claims.text: Elevated-temperature degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by competitive oxidation processes.
Al and Cr can contribute to protective oxidation or passivation behavior.
The alloy's low Al content prevents formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 scale.
Restricted Al2O3 formation permits preferential oxidation of Ti.
Ti oxidation is concentrated at grain boundaries.
Ti oxidation produces brittle TiO2 that tends to spall during thermal cycling.
TiO2 formation and spallation undermine the protective scale and material integrity.
Reducing atmospheres suppress formation of a robust external oxide film.
Suppression of the external scale under reducing conditions permits internal oxidation, primarily of Ti, along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary internal oxidation degrades microstructural cohesion and mechanical performance.
The as-fabricated alloy has a uniform, single-phase fcc matrix.
The fcc matrix provides the alloy's baseline strength, fatigue performance, and formability.
Exposure near 1200 °C produces mixed oxide scales at the surface and along grain boundaries.
Oxidizing exposure near 1200 °C will produce discontinuous Ti-rich oxide scales, spallation, and possible grain-boundary penetration.
Oxidizing exposure will measurably reduce mechanical performance relative to the pristine alloy.
Reducing exposure will produce less pronounced external scales but more internal Ti oxidation along grain boundaries.
The proposed mechanism is expected to dominate around 1200 °C in air-like oxidizing gases and moderately reducing gases.
Large changes in temperature or gas chemistry may activate alternative degradation pathways.
The as-fabricated baseline has no pre-existing oxide scale or internal oxidation features.
